title: Facade pattern
idea: The Facade pattern gives a set of collaborating classes one simple entry point that runs their steps in the right order, so callers stop orchestrating the parts themselves.
points: Without a facade, every caller repeats the call order and the cleanup on failure.
The facade owns the workflow: `placeOrder` reserves, charges, ships and undoes on failure.
Subsystem classes stay usable directly; a facade adds a shortcut, not a wall.
SLF4J is a logging facade. Skip one when callers only touch one class.

hero.title: One call, three subsystems, one cleanup

steps.caption: Both controllers make one call. Neither knows which subsystems exist behind `Checkout`.
Step 1: the facade reserves one unit. If none is left, it stops here.
Step 2: it charges the card. A decline releases the reserved unit at once.
Step 3: it books shipping. Success returns one `OrderResult` to the caller.
A shipping failure refunds the charge and releases stock. The cleanup lives in one place.

code.title: The problem: copied steps
code.caption: Two controllers each copy the checkout steps. One copy forgets to release stock.

walk.text: Three subsystems, each fine alone. The danger is in how callers combine them.
The web controller knows the order and the undo step. That knowledge is now copied.
The mobile copy drifted: on a decline it returns without releasing the reserved lamp.
One sale and one decline should leave 2 lamps. The leak shows in the output.
Each controller depends on three classes. A new step means editing every caller.

code.title: The fix: a Checkout facade
code.caption: One `placeOrder` call runs the steps in order and undoes them on failure.

walk.text: The facade gets its subsystems by constructor injection and rejects missing ones early.
Validate input first, then reserve. No stock is an expected outcome, not an exception.
A declined charge releases the reserved unit before returning a failed result.
A shipping failure undoes both earlier steps, newest first: refund, then release.
Callers get one small value object, not three subsystem return types.
Every client path now shares one tested workflow, so stock stays correct.

pitfalls: A facade that grows pricing, tax and email logic becomes a god class; keep it orchestrating.
Copying the facade's steps into a new caller brings back drift; route every caller through it.
Forcing all access through the facade blocks advanced callers; leave the subsystems usable directly.

quiz.q: `Checkout` calls `Inventory`, `Payments` and `Shipping`. `LegacyPaymentAdapter` wraps an old SDK. Which statement is right?
options: Both are facades, since both wrap other code
`Checkout` is a facade; the adapter converts one interface
`Checkout` is an adapter, since callers see a new interface
Both are proxies, since both forward calls
quiz.why: A facade simplifies many classes behind one new entry point. An adapter makes one existing class fit an interface the caller already expects.

takeaway: A facade turns a multi-step workflow over many classes into one safe call.
